slides: Welcome back, and now word problems. A word problem is a short story, with a question about it.

slides.say: The story can be about anything. A queue at a shop, a water tank, a trip, or friends sharing sweets. But under every story there's some math.

slides: Word problems are a big part of the quantitative section. Some questions are pure word problems. And many algebra and geometry questions are also written as a story. So this chapter pays off everywhere.

slides.say: We won't learn a trick for every story. We'll learn to see what's under it. Sometimes it's a total that's cut into parts. Sometimes it's a ratio. And sometimes it's just a short list of cases.
We start with the most down-to-earth tool there is, trial and error. Trial and error means we try, we get it wrong, and we try again. There's no equation and no formula.
Let's see it in numbers. A shop sells pens at three dollars and notebooks at five dollars. Dan spends exactly nineteen dollars, and he buys at least one of each. How many notebooks does he buy?

slides: What do we try? The notebooks, because there are fewer options. Four notebooks would already cost twenty dollars, more than nineteen. So Dan buys one, two or three notebooks. Let's try them in order.

slides.say: One notebook costs five dollars, so nineteen minus five leaves fourteen for the pens. Fourteen doesn't divide by three, because three times four is twelve and three times five is fifteen. So one notebook doesn't work.
Two notebooks cost ten dollars, so nineteen minus ten leaves nine. Nine divided by three is three pens. That works, two notebooks and three pens.
And three notebooks cost fifteen, which leaves four dollars. Four doesn't divide by three, so that's out too. We tried in order, so we know the list is complete. The only answer is two notebooks.
Now let's change one thing. Say Dan spends twenty dollars. One notebook leaves twenty minus five, fifteen. Fifteen divided by three is five pens. It works on the very first try.
at: One notebook leaves twenty minus five

slides: That's trial and error. Sometimes the first try works, and sometimes it takes a few. Each try is just a check against the story. And when we try in order, nothing gets lost. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
